title: Does Carbonation Make You Drunk Faster? What the Science Says
excerpt: Do bubbles get you drunk faster? How carbonation speeds alcohol absorption for many people, why diet mixers hit harder, what champagne research shows, and how to drink fizzy drinks sensibly.
metaDescription: Does carbonation make you drunk faster? How bubbles and diet mixers speed alcohol absorption, what the research shows, and how to slow it down.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: does carbonation make you drunk faster
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, carbonation can make you feel drunk faster, but not for everyone and not by a huge amount. The bubbles don't add any alcohol. What they seem to do, for many people, is push alcohol out of the stomach and into the small intestine sooner, which is where most of it gets absorbed into your blood. That means your blood alcohol rises a bit faster in the first half hour or so after a fizzy drink than it would after the same amount of alcohol in a flat drink. In the small studies that exist, most people showed this effect, while a minority showed no change or even slower absorption. The total amount of alcohol you take in stays the same. Bubbles change the timing, not the total.

**The quick version:** Champagne, prosecco, vodka soda, rum and Coke, gin and tonic, hard seltzer, and beer can all hit a little faster than a flat drink with the same alcohol. Diet mixers may hit faster still, because sugar slows the stomach down and diet soda has none. Food in your stomach matters far more than bubbles do. If you want fizzy drinks to treat you gently, eat first, sip rather than gulp, and count drinks rather than going by feel.

> **Safety note.** This article explains how alcohol absorption works. It is not medical advice. **Get emergency help (call 911 in the US) if someone** is confused or can't be woken, is vomiting while drowsy or passed out, is breathing slowly or irregularly (fewer than 8 breaths a minute or long gaps between breaths), has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. These are signs of alcohol poisoning. Don't let them "sleep it off," and don't leave them alone. If you're worried about what you or a friend drank, it is always fine to call.

## Does Carbonation Make You Drunker? What Actually Happens in Your Body

To understand why bubbles matter, it helps to know where alcohol actually goes after you swallow it.

### Most alcohol is absorbed in the small intestine, not the stomach

A common belief is that alcohol gets absorbed in your stomach. Some of it does, but only a modest share. The stomach lining absorbs alcohol slowly. The small intestine, just past the stomach, has an enormous surface area and a rich blood supply, and it absorbs alcohol very quickly. Most of the alcohol in a drink ends up in your bloodstream through the small intestine.

Between the stomach and the small intestine sits a ring of muscle called the **pyloric valve** (or pylorus). It works like a gate. When it's mostly closed, the drink sits in your stomach and trickles onward slowly. When it opens more, the contents move into the small intestine faster, and alcohol starts pouring into your blood.

This is why the speed at which your stomach empties, called **gastric emptying**, is one of the biggest factors in how quickly you feel a drink. Anything that speeds gastric emptying tends to make alcohol hit faster and peak higher. Anything that slows it, like a full meal, tends to make alcohol hit slower and peak lower.

### How bubbles fit in

Carbonated drinks contain dissolved carbon dioxide gas. When that gas comes out of solution in your warm stomach, it adds volume and pressure. The leading explanation for the carbonation effect is that this extra pressure and stretch nudges the stomach to empty sooner, moving alcohol into the small intestine earlier than a flat drink would.

There are a couple of other ideas researchers have raised, such as carbon dioxide directly increasing blood flow or absorption in the stomach lining. These are less well established. What matters for you is the practical result: in controlled tests, fizzy drinks often produce a faster early rise in blood alcohol.

### It changes the speed, not the amount

This point gets lost a lot. Carbonation does not create alcohol, and it doesn't make your liver slower at clearing it. Two drinks with the same alcohol content deliver the same total dose whether they're bubbly or flat. What can differ is the **shape of the curve**: a fizzy drink may produce a quicker rise and a slightly higher early peak, while a flat drink spreads the same alcohol out more gently.

That faster rise is what you feel as "this hit me fast." A higher peak also means a moment of greater impairment, which is why the effect matters for things like driving, even if the difference sounds small on paper. If you want a refresher on how blood alcohol is measured and what the numbers mean, see our guide to [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac).

## What the Research Says (and What It Doesn't)

The research on carbonation and alcohol is real but limited. The studies are small, and they don't all agree. Here's a fair picture.

### The vodka and fizzy water study

The best-known study comes from researchers at the University of Surrey in the UK, published in the *Journal of Forensic and Legal Medicine* in 2007 (Roberts and Robinson). Volunteers drank vodka on separate occasions, mixed either with still water or with carbonated water, along with neat vodka on another occasion. The researchers measured how quickly alcohol showed up in the volunteers' blood.

On average, the carbonated version was absorbed faster. But the more interesting finding was the spread between people. Roughly two-thirds of the volunteers absorbed the alcohol faster with the fizzy mixer, while the rest showed no increase or even absorbed it more slowly. In other words, carbonation sped things up for most people, but not for everyone.

The same study also looked at alcohol strength. Moderately diluted alcohol was absorbed faster than neat vodka for most people. That fits with another well-known pattern: very strong drinks can irritate the stomach and slow its emptying, while drinks in a middle range of strength move through more readily.

### The champagne study

Another small study, published in *Alcohol and Alcoholism* in 2003 (Ridout and colleagues), compared fizzy champagne with the same champagne that had been made flat. Volunteers who drank the bubbly version had higher blood alcohol levels in the first minutes after drinking, and they performed worse on some reaction and attention tests, than when they drank the flat version. By later time points, the difference had narrowed.

This lines up with what a lot of people notice at weddings and celebrations: the first glass of sparkling wine seems to land quickly. If champagne or prosecco is your usual drink, our guides to the [champagne hangover](/never-hungover/champagne-hangover-why-it-happens-prevention-guide) and the [prosecco hangover](/never-hungover/prosecco-hangover) cover the morning-after side.

### Why the results aren't the same for everyone

Several things can blunt or reverse the carbonation effect:

- **Food in the stomach.** A meal slows gastric emptying so much that it can swamp any effect of bubbles.
- **How fast you drink.** Bubbles can make some people sip more slowly, because fizzy drinks are filling and can cause burping or bloating. Slower drinking cancels out faster emptying.
- **Individual stomach behavior.** People's stomachs simply empty at different speeds, and they respond differently to gas and volume.
- **How flat the drink gets.** A drink that sits in a warm room and loses its fizz behaves more like a flat drink.

So the honest summary is this: there is reasonable evidence that carbonation speeds up alcohol absorption for many people, especially in the short window after drinking, but the effect varies and the studies are small. It's a real factor, not a myth, and not a dramatic one.

## Does Soda Make You Drunk Faster? Mixers Explained

A lot of people search this as "does soda make you drunk faster" or "does mixing alcohol with soda get you drunker." The answer depends on two things: the bubbles and the sugar.

### Bubbles push one way, sugar pushes the other

Regular sugary soda has carbonation, which may speed gastric emptying. But it also has sugar, and sugar tends to **slow** gastric emptying. Your stomach holds onto calorie-dense liquids longer so it can release them at a steady pace. So a rum and regular Coke has one factor speeding things up and another slowing things down.

Diet soda keeps the bubbles but removes the sugar. That leaves only the factor that speeds things up.

### The diet mixer research

This is one of the more consistent findings in the area. A study from Australia, published in the *American Journal of Medicine* in 2006 (Wu and colleagues), found that vodka mixed with an artificially sweetened mixer emptied from the stomach faster and produced higher blood alcohol levels than the same vodka with a sugar-sweetened mixer.

Later work from researchers at Northern Kentucky University, led by Cecile Marczinski and published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, found that people who drank alcohol mixed with diet soda had noticeably higher breath alcohol readings than when they drank the same amount of alcohol mixed with regular soda. They didn't necessarily feel more impaired, which is the worrying part. Their breath readings were higher than they realized.

The practical takeaway: a vodka and diet soda, a whiskey and Coke Zero, or a rum and diet cola may raise your blood alcohol faster and higher than the sugary version. That doesn't make sugary mixers "healthy," but it's a useful thing to know if you're the one picking the mixer and you're planning to drive later, or simply want to stay in control.

### Tonic, ginger ale, and club soda

- **Club soda and seltzer** have bubbles and no sugar, so they behave like diet mixers in this respect. A vodka soda is a classic "light" drink, and it's lower in calories, but it may also hit you sooner.
- **Tonic water** is carbonated and usually contains a fair amount of sugar, so it sits in the middle. Diet tonic behaves more like club soda.
- **Ginger ale and lemon-lime soda** are carbonated and sugary, like cola.

None of this changes how much alcohol is in your glass. A double vodka soda still has twice the alcohol of a single, and that matters far more than which mixer you chose. If you're wondering how sugary mixers affect the next morning, our guide to [soda for a hangover](/never-hungover/soda-for-hangover) covers that question.

## Do Bubbles Get You Drunk Faster? Drink by Drink

Here's how common fizzy drinks stack up. Keep in mind that alcohol content and how fast you drink are still the main factors.

### Champagne, prosecco, and cava

Sparkling wines are carbonated, cold, and easy to drink, and they're often served on an empty stomach at receptions before the food arrives. That combination is why sparkling wine has a reputation for going straight to your head. The bubbles likely play a part, but so do the empty stomach and the pace. A standard glass of sparkling wine at around 12% alcohol is roughly one standard drink, and topped-up flutes make it very easy to lose count.

### Beer

Beer is carbonated, but it's also relatively dilute, and many beers contain some carbohydrates and other compounds that may slow gastric emptying somewhat. People also tend to drink beer in larger volumes over longer periods. So the carbonation effect with beer is usually less noticeable than with a fizzy mixed drink. A strong craft beer or a quickly finished pint is a different story, simply because of the alcohol content and pace.

### Hard seltzer

Hard seltzers combine carbonation with very little sugar, which puts them on the "may absorb faster" side. They're typically around 5% alcohol, similar to a regular beer, so a single can isn't unusually strong. The risk is that they taste like flavored water and go down quickly, so people drink several in a short time without registering them.

### Mixed drinks with soda or tonic

Highballs like gin and tonic, vodka soda, Cuba libre, and Aperol spritz are carbonated, and many are served on ice in tall glasses that are easy to finish quickly. If the mixer is diet or unsweetened, expect a faster rise. If it's sugary, the sugar may partly offset the bubbles. Pour sizes at home are often much bigger than a bar's standard measure, which matters more than anything else on this list.

### Energy drink mixers

Many energy drinks are carbonated, and caffeine brings its own problem: it can make you feel more alert than you actually are, so you may keep drinking past the point where you'd normally slow down. Caffeine doesn't lower your blood alcohol. If you're mixing the two, be extra careful about counting drinks.

## Carbonation vs. Other Things That Make You Drunk Faster

Carbonation is only one factor, and not the biggest. Here's roughly how the main influences compare.

### Things that matter a lot

- **How much alcohol you drink.** Nothing beats this. Two strong cocktails can contain three or four standard drinks.
- **How fast you drink.** Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly steady rate, very roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults. Drinking faster than that makes blood alcohol climb, bubbles or not.
- **Whether you've eaten.** Food is the single best way to slow absorption. A meal, especially one with protein, fat, and fiber, keeps the pyloric valve closed longer and lowers the peak. Our guide to [drinking on an empty stomach](/never-hungover/drinking-on-an-empty-stomach) explains why skipping dinner makes such a difference.
- **Body size, body water, and sex.** Smaller people and people with less body water reach higher blood alcohol levels from the same drinks. Women, on average, reach higher levels than men from the same amount.

### Things that matter some

- **Carbonation**, as covered above.
- **Diet versus sugary mixers.**
- **Drink strength.** Moderately strong drinks may absorb faster than very dilute or very strong ones.
- **Medications and health conditions** that change how fast your stomach empties, including some acid reducers and conditions that cause slow stomach emptying.

### Things that don't matter (or barely do)

- **Drinking through a straw.** It only matters if it makes you drink faster. We break this down in [does a straw get you drunk faster](/never-hungover/does-a-straw-get-you-drunk-faster).
- **The order you drink in.** "Beer before liquor" is about pace and amount, not order. See our [beer before liquor myth](/never-hungover/beer-before-liquor-myth) explainer.
- **The type of glass.** A flute, a can, or a solo cup doesn't change chemistry, though some glass shapes can make you pour or drink more.

If you want a sense of how all these factors add up for your size and pace, our guide on [how many drinks it takes to get drunk](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-to-get-drunk) walks through it.

## Does Carbonation Make Hangovers Worse?

There's no good evidence that carbonation directly causes worse hangovers. A hangover is driven mainly by how much alcohol you drank in total, along with things like poor sleep, dehydration, stomach irritation, and how your body handles alcohol's by-products. Since carbonation doesn't change the total amount, it doesn't, by itself, change the size of the hangover.

That said, fizzy drinks can contribute indirectly in a few ways:

- **They're easy to drink quickly.** Faster drinking often means more drinks overall, and that does mean a worse morning.
- **Bloating and gas.** Carbon dioxide can leave you feeling bloated and uncomfortable, and some people find it adds to stomach upset after a night out.
- **Reflux.** Carbonated drinks can relax the valve at the top of the stomach and increase pressure, which may make heartburn and reflux worse for people who are prone to it. Alcohol does the same, so the two together can be rough on a sensitive stomach.
- **Sugary mixers late at night** can disrupt sleep for some people, and poor sleep makes hangovers feel worse.

So if bubbly drinks seem to give you worse hangovers, the likely culprits are pace and quantity rather than the bubbles themselves. For a full plan, see [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover).

## How to Enjoy Fizzy Drinks Without Getting Drunk Too Fast

You don't need to give up champagne toasts or gin and tonics. A few simple habits take most of the sting out of the carbonation effect.

1. **Eat before and while you drink.** This does more than any other step. Even a modest meal slows gastric emptying and softens the early spike.
2. **Sip the first drink slowly.** The carbonation effect is strongest in the first half hour. Making that first drink last is the single most useful thing you can do at a party.
3. **Alternate with water.** A glass of water or plain sparkling water between alcoholic drinks slows your overall pace. Yes, plain fizzy water is fine here, because there's no alcohol in it to speed up.
4. **Watch the top-ups.** At weddings and brunches, servers refill flutes before they're empty. Finish your glass before accepting another so you can actually count.
5. **Know your pours.** A home-poured vodka soda can easily be a double or triple. Use a jigger or ask for a standard measure.
6. **Be extra careful with diet mixers if you'll drive.** Better still, don't drive after drinking at all. Breath and blood alcohol can be higher than you feel, especially with diet mixers.
7. **Don't use "it's just bubbly" as a reason to skip counting.** A bottle of prosecco shared between two people is several drinks each.

For more ways to stay in control on a night out, see [how to not get drunk](/never-hungover/how-to-not-get-drunk), and if you're trying to judge when you'll be clear the next day, see [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up).

## When Getting Drunk Fast Becomes a Safety Problem

For most social drinkers, the carbonation effect just means the first drink feels a little stronger than expected. But the faster your blood alcohol rises, the less time you have to notice that you've had enough. That's why fast-acting drinks are a common part of nights that go wrong.

Take it seriously and get help right away if you or a friend:

- Can't be woken up, or keeps drifting out of consciousness
- Is confused, disoriented, or can't stand or speak clearly
- Is vomiting while drowsy or passed out
- Has slow, shallow, or irregular breathing
- Has a seizure
- Has pale, bluish, cold, or clammy skin

These are signs of alcohol poisoning, and they need emergency care. Call 911 (in the US) or your local emergency number. Turn the person on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, stay with them, and don't give them coffee or a cold shower to "sober them up." Blood alcohol can keep rising for a while after the last drink, especially after a round of fast-absorbing drinks, so someone who seems "fine for now" can get worse.

Also skip driving, swimming, or operating anything after drinking, even if you feel okay. A faster early rise in blood alcohol is exactly the situation where people underestimate how impaired they are.

## Where DHM Fits In

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound found in the Japanese raisin tree, and it's a popular ingredient in hangover supplements. It's worth being clear about what it can and can't do here.

DHM does **not** slow alcohol absorption, and it won't stop carbonation from making a drink hit faster. It won't lower your blood alcohol or make you safe to drive. There is no good evidence that it prevents getting drunk. The research interest in DHM is about how the body handles alcohol after it's absorbed: early studies, mostly in animals, suggest it may support alcohol metabolism and the liver, and some people find it helps them feel better the next morning. Human evidence is still limited.

If you'd like to try it as part of a sensible night (eating, pacing yourself, and drinking water), a straightforward option is [Double Wood Supplements DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), a single-ingredient DHM product. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how people typically take it, and you can compare options in our [supplement reviews](/reviews). Talk to your doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medication.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does carbonation make you drunk faster?**

For many people, yes, somewhat. Carbonation appears to speed up how quickly the stomach empties into the small intestine, where most alcohol is absorbed, so blood alcohol tends to rise faster in the first half hour or so. In small studies, most volunteers absorbed alcohol faster with a fizzy mixer, but some showed no change or slower absorption. The total amount of alcohol stays the same.

**Does carbonation make you drunker overall, or just faster?**

Mainly faster. Bubbles don't add alcohol or slow your liver. They can produce a quicker rise and sometimes a slightly higher early peak in blood alcohol, which you may feel as getting drunk faster. Over a whole evening, how drunk you get depends far more on how much you drink, how fast, and whether you've eaten.

**Does soda make you drunk faster than juice or water?**

It can. Carbonated mixers may speed absorption compared with flat ones. Sugary soda is a mixed case because sugar slows stomach emptying, which partly offsets the bubbles. Diet soda and club soda keep the bubbles without the sugar, and research has found diet mixers produce higher blood or breath alcohol than sugary mixers with the same amount of alcohol.

**Why does champagne go straight to my head?**

A few things combine. The bubbles may speed absorption, and a small study found higher blood alcohol in the first minutes after fizzy champagne compared with the same champagne made flat. Sparkling wine is also often served on an empty stomach, drunk quickly during toasts, and topped up before glasses are empty, so it's easy to have more than you realize.

**Do diet mixers really get you drunker?**

They can raise blood alcohol faster and higher than sugary mixers. Studies published in the American Journal of Medicine (2006) and Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research (2013) found higher alcohol levels with artificially sweetened mixers. In the 2013 study, people didn't necessarily feel more impaired, which makes it easy to underestimate your level. This matters most if you're thinking about driving, which you shouldn't do after drinking anyway.

**Does beer get you drunk faster because it's carbonated?**

Usually not by much. Beer is carbonated, but it's relatively dilute and contains carbohydrates that may slow stomach emptying, and people tend to drink it over longer periods. Strong beers or pints finished quickly can still raise blood alcohol fast, mostly because of the alcohol content and pace.

**Does letting a drink go flat make it less intoxicating?**

It may slightly slow how fast the alcohol is absorbed, but the total amount of alcohol is unchanged. A flat drink still delivers the same dose. Eating, sipping slowly, and having fewer drinks are much more effective ways to stay in control.

**Is drinking carbonated water with alcohol a bad idea?**

Not as a separate glass between drinks. Plain sparkling water has no alcohol, and alternating it with alcoholic drinks slows your overall pace, which helps. Using soda water as a mixer can speed absorption of the alcohol in that same glass a little, so sip mixed drinks rather than gulping them.

**Can DHM stop bubbles from making me drunk faster?**

No. DHM does not slow alcohol absorption or lower blood alcohol, and there is no good evidence that it prevents intoxication. Research on DHM focuses on alcohol metabolism and liver support after drinking, mostly from animal studies. The way to blunt the carbonation effect is to eat first, drink slowly, and count your drinks.
